title: The supernova impostor: Chandra finds likely source of giant star's repeated outbursts
excerpt: Using NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory, astronomers have discovered what is triggering repeated outbursts from a giant, unstable star.
content:
Using NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory, astronomers have discovered what is triggering repeated outbursts from a giant, unstable star.

A new paper, published in the latest issue of The Astrophysical Journal, details the discovery of a previously hidden companion object that keeps pulling material away from the massive star every 113 days as they orbit one another. This partner is either a stellar-mass black hole or the dense collapsed core of a massive star called a neutron star.

This is the first X-ray detection of one of this class of erupting stars. It is also the first of these objects found with a black hole or neutron star companion.

The volatile star, known as AT 2016blu, is in the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, located about 30 million light-years from Earth. Astronomers estimate the mass of this star is at least 33 times that of the sun.

"For 15 years, astronomers have been watching this star get really bright and then dim again on a regular basis," said Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia in Charlottesville, who led this study. "Until we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldn't figure out what was making this happen."

The star AT 2016blu is a type of luminous blue variable, a hot, massive star characterized by large changes in brightness. Eta Carinae, for example, is a particularly well-known luminous blue variable. AT 2016blu is a special type of luminous blue variable that undergoes rapid and repeated increases in brightness. The spikes in brightness are so extreme that they resemble supernova explosions, where a massive star collapses onto itself and material then hurtles outward into space.
